116	\paragraph{AUC decay profile.}
117	Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} plots the binary pairwise AUC decay curves.
118	For Pythia-1.4B (nucleus), AUC decays monotonically: d0-vs-d1 $= 0.999$, d1-vs-d2 $= 0.925$, d2-vs-d3 $= 0.823$, d3-vs-d4 $= 0.784$, d4-vs-d5 $= 0.683$.
119	The steepest drop occurs between the d1-vs-d2 and d2-vs-d3 pairs; the curve then flattens as the system approaches an indistinguishable regime gradually rather than crossing a sharp boundary.
120	
121	\paragraph{Geometric decay model.}
122	The monotonic AUC decay is well approximated by a geometric model $\mathrm{AUC}(d, d{+}1) = A_0 \cdot \gamma^d$, where $A_0$ is the d0-vs-d1 AUC and $\gamma$ is the per-step retention factor.
123	A least-squares fit to the Pythia-1.4B nucleus curve yields $\gamma \approx 0.74$ ($R^2 = 0.97$), predicting AUC values $0.995, 0.953, 0.862, 0.766, 0.683$ for $d{=}0$--$4$ (observed: $0.999, 0.925, 0.823, 0.784, 0.683$).
124	The model captures the overall trajectory while slightly overestimating mid-range AUC, consistent with the steeper empirical drop at d1-vs-d2.
125	
126	\paragraph{Cross-model convergence at depth 4--5.}
127	The d3-vs-d4 AUC consistently clusters near the $T{=}0.75$ threshold across all three models (Pythia $0.784$, OLMo $0.765$, GPT-2~XL $0.750$), while d4-vs-d5 uniformly falls below $0.70$ ($0.681$--$0.684$).
128	The directional pattern is consistent, but statistical strength is stratified: bootstrap testing ($10{,}000$ resamples, $H_0{:}\, \mathrm{AUC} \leq 0.75$) yields $p = 0.001$ for Pythia (significant), $p = 0.091$ for OLMo (marginal), and $p = 0.505$ for GPT-2~XL (non-significant).
129	All three models cross the $T{=}0.75$ threshold within the d3--d4 region, establishing a consistent depth-4 decay boundary with graded confidence rather than uniform statistical significance.
130	The d4-vs-d5 saturation is unambiguous across models, supporting the interpretation of d3--d4 as a \emph{transition zone} from discriminable to indistinguishable regime.
```

    "originalFile": "\\section*{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}\nCross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.\nPer-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion under logistic regression (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\\to}0.70$) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments ($\\Delta < 0.02$\\,pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\\sim}0.83$), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.\n\n\\paragraph{Strategy-unknown deployment.}\nIn strategy-unknown settings, naive transfer on d1--d3 yields only 45.9\\%, and d1/d2 predictions may invert.\nA two-stage pipeline recovers 11.5\\,pp over LOO, though per-model gains vary (GPT-2~XL $+$16.4\\,pp vs.\\ Pythia $+$8.0\\,pp).\nPractical deployment requires either strategy metadata or learned routing.\n\n\\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}\nDepth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$98\\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.\nCross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).\n\n\\paragraph{Controlled vs.\\ ecological setting.}\nThe primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled LoRA fine-tuning (1--1.5B models), isolating the depth variable but diverging from wild contamination where models train on mixed corpora with prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions.\nDomain bias controls confirm depth as the dominant factor: LOGO accuracy (72.1\\%) matches standard CV (72.0\\%), seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\\%; Appendix~\\ref{app:domain_bias}).\nCross-scale experiments (7--8B, \\S\\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) show weaker but above-chance signal; a base-model control suggests instruction-tuning regularizes degradation.\nSegment-level estimation in mixed-depth documents remains open.\n\n\\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}\nOn editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\\geq$98.5\\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), per-model FPR ranges from 4.7\\% (OLMo) to 22.4\\% (GPT-2~XL).\nA pooled RF classifier evaluated on larger corpora (10{,}000 passages each) yields 34\\% FPR on C4 and 17\\% on FineWeb; the gap reflects quality filtering in FineWeb removing feature-anomalous text, not differences in recursive contamination prevalence.\nMisclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\\texttt{rep\\_3gram} $+$37\\%, \\texttt{rep\\_4gram} $+$75\\% vs.\\ correctly classified d0).\nDeployment on heterogeneous web corpora requires model- and domain-specific calibration.\n\n\\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}\nAdversarial paraphrasing \\cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.\n\n\\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}\nOur EDD definition (Eq.~\\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically, as observed in all our configurations.\nHowever, \\citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \\emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).\nOur cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.\nIn such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.\nThe choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.\n\n\\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}\nReference model choice affects classification accuracy by up to 11\\,pp; same-family references yield optimal performance, though all configurations exceed $2.5\\times$ chance.\nSurprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators.\nFor the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2~XL measurements are cross-model.\nEmpirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.7\\% vs.\\ GPT-2~XL 85.9\\%), suggesting the overlap does not confer a systematic advantage.\nAn ablation with OLMo-1B and GPT-2 XL as alternative references shows accuracy ranging from 67--79\\% across three reference architectures (Appendix~\\ref{app:ref_ablation}), all exceeding $2.5\\times$ chance; same-family reference yields optimal performance ($\\Delta{\\leq}$11\\,pp).\nThe choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.\nReference-free surface features alone achieve 53.7\\% (confirming partial signal in lexical statistics) but 25pp below the full pipeline, underscoring that surprisal-based features are essential.\nSimple multi-reference ensembling does not outperform the best single reference (73.7\\% vs.\\ 78.6\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Single LoRA instance.}\nIndependent replication with seed=43 yields 77.15\\% (95\\% CI [76.4, 78.15], $\\Delta{=}{-}1.05$\\,pp vs.\\ baseline); 555	Training loss decreases monotonically with depth (d0: 2.558, d1: 1.920, d2: 1.286), consistent with recursive generation reducing information content and making text easier to model.
556	This pilot establishes that depth-filtered data is not harmful for downstream fine-tuning; whether depth-aware curation provides a meaningful advantage requires larger-scale evaluation.
557	
558	\subsection{Extended Discussion}
559	\label{app:extended_discussion}
560	
561	\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation.}
562	Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
563	Recursive generation depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) whose distributional properties remain close to the human source, while down-weighting or filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
564	The 70--85\% in-distribution accuracy and $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ suggest depth-graduated filtering is feasible within known model--strategy configurations, though the d1/d2 boundary inversion under cross-strategy transfer (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) means reliable curation requires either known decoding strategy metadata or an upstream strategy-identification step; a pilot study (Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}) yields an inconclusive RF-vs-unfiltered comparison ($p>0.4$), though RF-filtered subsets significantly outperform size-matched random subsampling ($p<0.001$--$0.02$); large-scale validation remains open.
565	Importance weighting \cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting} could further enable continuous depth-aware data selection rather than discrete thresholding.
566	
567	\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}
568	Depth estimation complements existing provenance methods along orthogonal axes.
569	Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} provides high-confidence attribution when the generator cooperates but is inapplicable to unwatermarked text.
570	Source attribution \cite{uchendu2020_attribution} identifies the generating model but not the generation history.
571	Depth estimation characterizes \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator cooperation or identity.
572	A layered provenance system combining these three signals (watermark presence, source model, and recursive generation depth) could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.
573	
```
